about_blocks: Begin With the Land and the People Connected to It

A royalty file starts with the record owner, family or entity history, county, legal description, deed or probate path, lease, division order, operator, payor, wells, products, and recent statement. Those facts explain which property and which economic right are under discussion.
Treat Family Fractions as a Trail, Not a Footnote

Mineral ownership often passes through generations, trusts, marriages, estates, reservations, and partial transfers. The desk maps that trail before assuming a check decimal or old family understanding describes the complete interest.
Read the Revenue as Evidence From a Particular Time

Royalty statements show products, volumes, prices, taxes, deductions, adjustments, suspense, and the decimal a payor currently recognizes. They help explain cash flow, but they do not replace recorded title or predict every future month.
Separate What Pays Today From What Might Be Drilled

Producing wells can be studied through history, decline, downtime, workovers, pricing, and operator decisions. Future development depends on permits, spacing, offsets, capital, service conditions, commodity outlook, and timing. Those value sources stay distinct.
Compare the Transaction Behind the Headline Number

Price belongs beside the exact interest description, included depths and formations, effective date, title standard, adjustment formula, diligence period, warranties, funding conditions, retained rights, and treatment of revenue before closing.
Carry the Same Property Through Closing

The purchase agreement, title schedule, conveyance exhibit, settlement calculation, signer authority, recording package, payor notice, and post-closing revenue handoff should all identify the same interest. A clear close honors both the owner and the land record.

resources: Turn the Guide Into a File Check

Use Each Record for What It Proves
The documents discussed in {name} may describe payment, title, lease burden, well history, or transaction terms. A useful review does not ask one record to prove everything.
Production, prices, deductions, decimals, permits, operator plans, and offers change. For {name}, every figure should retain its source, date, unit, period, and whether it is observed or forecast.
investing: Build the Producing Case From the Revenue Deck

For {name}, the buyer should begin with well-level volumes, products, realized prices, severance and property taxes, gathering or processing deductions, owner decimals, downtime, adjustments, and the dates represented by each statement. Gross regulatory production and net owner revenue are not interchangeable. The bridge between them should show unit allocation, lease burden, product mix, post-production costs, and the payor's current setup. Keeping that bridge dated also prevents a suspense release, correction, or one-time adjustment from being mistaken for ordinary monthly cash flow.
Treat Decline as a Range, Not a Clock

A decline case for {name} is an informed estimate shaped by completion design, pressure behavior, choke strategy, offset interference, artificial lift, workovers, curtailment, operating practice, and data gaps. The buyer's file should state the history used, forecast start date, decline method, terminal behavior, downtime allowance, and sensitivity range. If a producing history is short or interrupted, the uncertainty should widen instead of being hidden behind a smoother curve. That distinction matters to a family comparing a current check with a long-term lump-sum proposal.
Keep Future Development in a Separate Layer

{name} may involve permits, spacing, offset results, undeveloped benches, infill locations, recompletions, or operator inventory. Each possibility needs a formation, location count or probability, timing case, production shape, burden, price deck, capital and service context, and discount rate. Undeveloped possibility should not quietly inflate the producing cash flow or be described as a certainty. A clean review shows which dollars come from existing wells, which come from identified projects, and which depend on a broader basin story.

A useful review of {name} changes benchmark price, basin differential, product mix, gathering, compression, processing, transportation, marketing, taxes, and other deductions in separate cases. A buyer may be optimistic about commodity price but conservative about netback, or the reverse. Showing those variables individually makes the offer easier to compare with the owner's actual statement and helps explain why two proposals built from the same recent check can still differ. The family should be able to see which assumption moved rather than being handed a single unexplained multiple.
Show the Discount, Title Reserve, and Closing Math

The analysis for {name} should identify forecast periods, discount convention, terminal treatment, title reserve, data limitations, operator concentration, development timing, commodity sensitivity, and closing adjustments. It should also connect the modeled interest to the tract schedule, included depths, effective date, revenue cutoff, curative requirements, and final conveyance. The output is a buyer's underwriting case rather than an appraisal or investment recommendation. Facts, forecasts, and transaction terms remain labeled so later changes can be understood instead of appearing as a surprise reduction at closing.
exchange-1031: Confirm the Exchange Question Before Reshaping the Sale

For {name}, an owner should ask a qualified intermediary, attorney, and tax adviser whether the relinquished interest, replacement property, taxpayer, vesting, timing, related parties, debt, and proposed structure fit the owner's circumstances. Royalty Buyer can provide accurate transaction facts, dates, schedules, and draft documents, but the desk should not promise qualification or choose tax elections for a family. That advice boundary belongs in the working file from the first conversation so a proposed exchange does not quietly become an unsupported condition of the mineral sale.
Keep the Royalty Underwriting File Intact

A possible exchange does not change the need to identify the counties, tracts, interests, wells, depths, formations, fractions, effective date, title standard, adjustments, and retained rights in {name}. The buyer's production and development assumptions should remain documented even when proceeds routing and replacement-property timing receive extra attention. The family should still be able to trace the sale amount to the property being conveyed, the revenue being transferred, and the title findings that affect closing.
Coordinate the Intermediary Before Funds Move

The working file for {name} should identify the current owner, proposed seller, purchasing entity, qualified intermediary, escrow or closing agent, legal and tax advisers, assignment language, notice requirements, estimated consideration, expected adjustments, and intended proceeds path. Those parties and documents should be confirmed before the mineral sale closes or funds are released. If vesting, signer authority, entity names, or account instructions do not match, the discrepancy should be resolved before a deadline forces the parties into hurried paperwork.
Run One Calendar for the Sale and One for the Exchange

{name} can involve offer expiration, purchase-agreement signing, title review, curative work, adjustment deadlines, deed execution, mineral closing, intermediary assignment, the 45-day identification period, and the 180-day acquisition period. Placing every event on one page helps the owner see where buyer diligence, title work, replacement-property research, financing, and adviser approvals can collide. The calendar should show responsible parties, required documents, dependencies, and backup dates rather than treating the two statutory periods as the only deadlines that matter.
Preserve a Clear Non-Exchange Closing Path

A family considering {name} should understand what happens if the exchange proceeds, changes, or does not occur. The purchase agreement, deed, title schedule, settlement statement, revenue allocation, and buyer funding conditions still need to function as a mineral sale. A documented backup path does not provide tax advice, but it prevents unclear exchange assumptions from making the underlying conveyance vague. It also lets advisers focus on the owner's tax choices without forcing the buyer to rewrite the property description or closing economics at the last moment.
